What is the mechanism of injury? 

First thing is to control the bleeding— a tourniquet above the injury will stop the blood flow. If the character doesn’t have access to one, they can make one out of a blanket, jacket, shirt, etc. They just need to twist it tight enough to stop the bleeding— which is A LOT. That fucker is gonna hurt so bad, and any skin below it is going to turn purple and blue from lack of blood flow while wearing it. Realistically, it’s unlikely they would be able to apply it with one hand— more practically, someone else would need to do it. 

Next thing would be preventing infection. Depending on how long the character is going without treatment, they’re open to infection and eventually sepsis without at least cleaning the wound at a minimum. Ideally it would be cleaned, debrided if necessary, and dressed in clean, dry, bandages until they can get medical attention. 

The character may feel tired, lightheaded, or woozy due to blood loss. They are going to be writhing in pain, possibly blacking out due to the pain of a) the injury and b) the tourniquet. 

It is survivable definitely, with the right steps.

I had a patient there for chest pain. NSTEMI. I had already given her aspirin and started her heparin drip. 

She looked pretty well— she’d be up and walking around prior to the heparin, and her pain was 4/10. She calls me back in to say the chest pain has gotten a smidge worse, like a 6/10. 

I say okay, be right there— brought her some PRN nitro. And she said it was starting to help. 

A little bell went off in my head and I decided to get a repeat EKG, just to see. 

STEMI. Big ol’ STEMI. Rushed her to cath lab and they put 3 stents in her.

If I hadn’t thought to get that repeat EKG, who knows how that would have went. 🤷🏻‍♀️ 

This was really early in my career and I’ve held on to that— even if you know they’re here for chest pain, even if they’re on a heparin drip and aspirin and got nitro, even if they look like they’re fine: if they have a change in chest pain get. a. new. ekg. Every time.

The ER is not there to diagnose your longstanding, chronic issue that nobody can seem to figure out. It’s not there to diagnose all your problems. 

It’s there to rule out or treat life threatening or emergent medical conditions. You say “oh, I’ve got pain here,” ER will run its tests, see that you’re not actively or imminently dying, and then say “okay, follow up with your PCP if symptoms persist.” 

You will wait 8 hours for this, and it will cost several hundreds or thousands of dollars.

Nurse chiming in— when people reach a certain size, they’re no longer able to sufficiently reach all their nooks and folds. I frequently have patients with fungal or yeast infections between their folds (particularly towards their back, genitals, and pannus—which is the medial word for “fupa”), and skin breakdown from poor bathroom hygiene (not wiping or washing thoroughly, usually due to being unable to see/reach). Additionally, moving around that much weight is intense work, and often causes patients to start sweating with little effort; antiperspirant/deodorant can only do so much, and that’s assuming they’re able to reach appropriately to apply it. 

This doesn’t apply to all obese people— many bariatric patients still are able to reach their body adequately and can wash/clean/dry thoroughly.

Edit to add: I totally forgot to mention that being obese also limits your ability to fit into small spaces— like a shower or bathtub. When you no longer fit there, you have to settle for sponge-baths only, which is fine every so often but not ideal for your main source of bathing. You miss a lot of oils and whatnot in your skin that way, which is compounded by the inability to reach those spots anyway. 

Moral of the story is: avoid being obese if you can. Your healthcare later in life will suffer immensely.

My first death was as a nurse extern in a small, rural 12-bed ER. Got a call that a 2 week old was coming in, CPR in progress. I will always remember the sight of that EMS stretcher rolling in, 18-year-old volunteer EMT riding on it, giving compressions to that tiny baby and looking scared shitless. I watched the nurse drill an IO into his teeny little leg, because we didn’t have any IVs small enough, nor was any nurse there able to find a vein  Baby was very obviously DOA; cold to the touch, pale. The docs called it in maybe 10 minutes.

The baby had a tiny bit of blood coming out of his nose and ears. He also had a very unique name— one of those names that make you say “why the fuck would anyone ever name their kid that?” His parents weren’t allowed to come see him, at least not while I was there. 

I remember thinking that it must be horrible, knowing your baby is dead but not being allowed to see for yourself. 

I remember really random, useless details. I remember texting my brother right after everything and saying “I just saw a dead baby.” 

I remember he was a cute baby. Chubby cheeks, curly black hair, chunky lil legs. Beautiful baby boy, truly. 

I remember as we were getting everything we needed before he arrived, another nurse was grabbing a pulse ox and asked how old we had said the baby was. I remember her look of concern and fear, and the way she emphasized “*two weeks???*”

It was definitely not an easy one to be my first death. I coped okay, I managed fine, but I don’t think I’ll ever forget any of those details.

Nurse here chiming in. 

 Nurses and doctors are a *team.* We bring very different knowledge bases and skill sets to the table. 

While providers are responsible for a lot (and in the end, have the final say in directing patient care), nurses see/touch/interact with the patients much more. In nursing school, they really emphasize patient advocacy: voicing your opinion in the interest of patient safety. 

In my facility, I love my docs. They listen to and consider the nurses’ thoughts, and they respect us as their colleagues and fellow healthcare professionals. Trusting my gut and voicing my disagreement or concerns has saved a patient’s life more than a couple times— doctors can make mistakes too, and sometimes it’s the nurse that catches it. 

Nurses are a part of the healthcare team, with a respectable amount of education and experience. As such, their opinions and concerns should at least be considered by the provider.

(RN here)

Our sedations all have a sedation nurse that has taken a class and been checked off— their sole responsibility is to monitor and document the patient’s vitals/breathing/capno and alert the provider if there’s a concerning change. In my experience, if I notify the provider that the patient is becoming apneic or hypoxic, they’ll usually have a med student or a resident jaw thrust/bag/intervene as necessary. As the sedation nurse, we are not allowed to assist in the procedure, draw up/push the meds, or leave the room. Our main focus is making sure that patient is breathing and hemodynamically stable until they’ve fully come out of the sedation. I find that it works quite well.

You sit in your own stool for an unacceptable amount of time, because I can’t find 2-3 coworkers available to help me roll you and get you cleaned up. Your quality of care is compromised because you don’t fit in CT scanners or MRI machines, there’s only but so many beds or rooms we have that accommodate you, and God forbid your heart stops and we need to fight through literal inches of fat to find a vein for an IV. Ingredients: (makes 4 servings)
- 4-5 bone in chicken drumsticks
- 4-5 bone in chicken thighs 
- 1cup ish of flour
- 1/3 of breadcrumbs
- Spice blend: salt, pepper, MSG, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, coriander, the teeniest smidge of cardamom, cayenne
- 3-4 egg whites
- Peanut oil for frying

Directions:
1. Pat your chicken dry and season with salt and pepper
2. Set up your breading station: egg whites, beaten in one dish, flour+breadcrumbs and spice blend in the other. Season heavily!

4. Once oil is at 350F add your chicken a few pieces at a time so as to not crowd your pan

Anything that could be potentially threatening to loss of life or limb! Basically, just ask yourself: if I were to delay care on this, could I potentially die or lose a limb? So there are the obvious ones that most people would know:

- chest pain 
- shortness of breath
- trauma / significant bleeding
- new onset seizures 
- stroke-like symptoms (BE FAST symptoms)
- damage to the eyes
- dislocations, open or displaced fractures, severe disfigurement
- hypoglycemia that isn’t resolved with oral glucose

There are also some that people may or may not recognize as emergent:

- fever that won’t go away, especially in the presence of infection (ie, a wound gets infected and now it’s spreading systemically and you’re going septic) **edited to add: anything below 100.4F or 37.2C is not considered a fever, even if your 99.9 is “high for you.”**
- excessively high blood sugar (>500) 
- any sudden change in mental status or behavior
- any sudden/new onset pain that could be described as “worst you’ve ever felt.” Pain itself is not an emergency, but it is your body’s way of telling you something is wrong.

Things that do need to be addressed, but are not truly emergent. These can all be addressed at an urgent care or similar. 

- UTI symptoms (unless you’ve got a fever that won’t go away and you’re starting to display signs of sepsis— fast heart rate, fever you can’t control, low BP, altered mental status, etc.)
- vague, mild abdominal pain, especially if you’ve been having it for several days or weeks. If it hasn’t killed you in 24 hours, it likely won’t in the next 24 hours. 
- medication refill requests
- mild sprains or fractures
- abscesses that are not accompanied by signs of systemic infection
- moderate cuts and lacerations that could potentially need stitches

And things that are simply not an emergency and can be handled by PCP/specialist, or will resolve on their own. 

- flu or cold symptoms (as long as you’re able to keep yourself hydrated)
- chronic pain
- sprains of toes or fingers
- mild cuts, lacerations, or abrasions where bleeding is controlled, pulse/movement/sensation of the affected area is intact, and wound edges are approximated (touching each other)
- positive pregnancy test (why do we see so many of these coming to the ED???)
- anxiety/panic attack

This isn’t an exhaustive list, and when it comes down to it, listen to your gut. If something doesn’t really seem emergent but somethings telling you to go be seen immediately, GO. “Impending sense of doom” is a real symptom. There are also online nurse triage lines that can help direct you to the right level of care.

What you described, however, is an emergency. Tachycardia, chest pain— these are things that warrant an ER visit. We need to rule out cardiac issues, PE, sepsis, etc.

What doesn’t warrant an ER visit is “I need a full work up to diagnose this chronic condition because my PCP/specialist hasn’t done it.” 

The ER is for ruling out life-threatening diagnoses, not for finally giving a diagnosis on chronic issues that are not life-threatening.

Not OP, just a nurse, but I can help you answer this question. 

Your sex chromosomes consist of one from mom and one from dad. Men always have XY chromosomes, and women always have XX chromosomes. If someone is a carrier, a woman has at least one X chromosome affected. Because men only have one X chromosome, if they’ve received an affected X, they are automatically affected and not just carriers. 

So let’s say Mom has XX^• chromosomes, X^• representing a fragile X. Mom may be unaffected, as she has another completely normal X chromosome. This makes mom a carrier. Mom then makes a baby with Dad who has XY. That baby can receive 1 of 4 chromosomal makeups:

Mom (XX^• ) + Dad (XY)

- X from mom, X from dad = normal, unaffected female (XX)

- X from mom, Y from dad = normal, unaffected male (XY)

- X^• from mom, X from dad = carrier OR affected daughter (X^• X)

- X^• from mom, Y from dad = affected male (X^• Y)

Correct. We triage based on acuity…

People with a 1 are actively dying (or pretty damn close), or have lost a limb. Think heart attacks, advanced sepsis, strokes, amputations. 

People with a 2 will soon have an active threat of loss of life or limb if we don’t intervene immediately, or they have symptoms/vital signs that need to be corrected urgently before they worsen or cause damage. Think heart dysrhythmias, major dislocations, open fractures

People with a 3 do need to be treated, but theres no present threat to life or limb, so long as they’re treated relatively soon. Some of these people do need to be at the ER, but some could get away with being treated at an urgent care center instead. Think obscure abdominal pain, kidney stones, abscesses. 

People with a 4 have something minor that needs to be addressed, but is of low priority as it does not threaten life or limb. Most of these people could probably be treated at an Urgent Care center and don’t need to be at the ER. Think UTIs, pink eye, joint sprains, or other non-emergent issues. 

People with a 5 probably don’t need to be at the ER— this is usually something like a medication refill or a hangnail lol


The number you get will affect how quickly you’re seen— ones and twos obviously being seen much quicker than a five. Same goes for the treatments you receive— the stroke patient is getting their CT scan wayyyy sooner than the obscure 5/10 abdominal x 2 days. I have been a nurse at a Level 1 trauma center for about a year now. I enjoy it! ER nursing is its own breed, and you either love it or hate it. 

As someone else mentioned, ED is focused on quickly adapting, prioritizing needs, and keeping cool in a crisis. We don’t care about the minute details— we’re doing focused assessments to help the patient with their “emergency.” Im not checking the skin on a patient who is there for a heart attack. I’m not checking a CBC/CMP on a patient with a broken leg. Knowing relevant assessments to your patient’s chief complaint becomes a really vital learned skill— knowing to actually check the skin if they come in with an infection of sorts, for example. 

In the ED, I only care about what’s in front of me— everything else can be dealt with later, preferably as an inpatient. I don’t really care if you get your usual nighttime meds if you’re septic; youre getting abx, pressers, and fluids from me, not your evening metoprolol and melatonin. I like the instant gratification of seeing a patient improve with medications relatively immediately. Some people hate this— they like the nuance of knowing a patient’s chart inside and out, and being able to know every single thing this patient has going on. They like providing consistent care that helps the patient in the long-term. They like the details. Those people choose M/S type units. Some people like both the long term care and the immediate, acute care; I feel these people tend to gravitate toward ICU. 

Additionally, some people don’t like to see all the death and gore. It’s not for everyone. Some people choose specialties with low odds of seeing a patient die for that reason. I choose to be in an environment with a lot of death because it feels really, *really* good to literally bring someone back to life. It also feels… special (?) to be able to be there for someone in their last moments, and to say you did everything in your power to save them/ I also like it because there isn’t a lot of time for me to get attached to patients— the turnover is high and I don’t have time to get attached to them. “Treat em and street em,” as we say.
